en: The sentence of those already condemned,
He dealt with his own hands.
He was a giant surpassing champions,
Regarding others as less than a hair;
If you ask about that madman’s nature,
He was truly the master of strife.
Young Seytek, the fierce hero,
Steeling himself to valor,
Came forth, that fierce lion,
Leaning on his tempered-steel spear.
As brave Seytek stood there,
Ready to die if hostile death arrived,
To stand as a shield
For the descendants left to Seytek,
To challenge Sarybai,
And bring the battle to its appointed hour,
To save the surviving line
From the wrathful enemy’s hand,
“You have thrown my people into despair.
You left me alive without taking vengeance,
Me, brave Külchoro.
You made him renowned across the earth,
You made Sarybai a hero,
But Külchoro the lion—
Why have you humbled him so?
Casting him so often before hostile death,
Why have you brought him so low?
You made Sarybai mighty;
Damn you, treacherous world,
Why have you so disgraced
This head of a true fierce lion?
You shamelessly let me be bound,
My two arms of a lion’s strength;
You let my robe be taken as spoil,
And visited this wonder upon my head.
Take me, God, without tormenting me,
Without wearing me down in helplessness.
Do not disgrace me before the multitude,
Do not, before this settled nation,
Make Sarybai so mighty.”
So lamented Külchoro,
Grieving as he named reedy Кең-Кол and broad Talas,
Counting over every tract of land,
Grieving for the joyous Kyrgyz, his ancestral people,
Counting over all the tribes.
He could not die though he yearned to,
Could not take his own life,
Could not restrain the tears in his eyes,
Nor gather once again
His valiant Kyrgyz, his beloved people.
Unless the Almighty willed it,
He could not go to death himself.
He came to the gray hills and made ready,
Leaning upon his gray spear,
And halted at the great gate,
Lamenting an ancient grief.
Six thousand camels and countless colts,
The white tent bought at great price,
Lions afraid and all the people weeping—
A savage conflict arose.
The hero despaired of life,
The people cried aloud in grief,
Black night descended on the nation,
And Sarybai alone became a demon of hell.
Külchoro, once aided by the spirit,
Leant against Üch-Koshoy.
Wounded in ninety places,
His body drenched in blood,
Beneath the hero
Six thoroughbred horses had died.
His strength exhausted, he staggered,
And the spirit-aided hero
Stood there dumbfounded.
Damn you, treacherous world,
Filthy world that lives by deceit—
Your deception has proven true.
You cast misery upon mortals;
Sarybai, son of the ogress,
Was the one I lacked the strength to overcome,
Yet you made him a champion and a lion.
At the very end, filthy world,
You made Sarybai a hero.
You bent my precious falcon head,
O treacherous world,
And laid it level with the black earth.
You made his strength as vast as mountains;
Unable to prevail against Sarybai,
You plunged me into grim despair.
Fate that created and ordained me,
Calling me a lion among warriors,
You made me a crag like Alaskar.
Yet in the end, Almighty,
The descendants of the countless Kyrgyz,
The heirs of the khan’s son—
You took away the people’s hope,
And disgraced before Sarybai
The sons of Almambet and Manas.
You bent my back low,
Wiser than all who came before,
When foes arrived in countless thousands,
He would ride forth to meet them.
His guardian was the gray tiger;
No such soul existed beneath a saddle girth.
Brave Semetey, the great sultan,
Surpassed all others in valor.
The infidel son of the ogress,
The warrior who made the earth tremble,
He resisted without rest for seven days.
At Echoing Jar-Kyya,
On a path fit for only one horse,
In a gorge no steed could pass,
In a foul place of bitter winds,
He grappled with Sarybai,
Enduring grim hardship and night.
He saw venomous courage and harsh days,
The hero saw ridges and trials,
And met a notorious warrior of hell.
“So this is the son of the ogress;
My direst foe has emerged,
And my true skill has been revealed.
My armor is torn and my arms are spent—
O hell, can such a thing be?
Does this wrathful madman
Spare anyone who grapples with him?
My spear is shattered, my strength gone,
My power exhausted, my day finished;
The ogress’s son has worn me down.
My appointed time has come.
You who first shaped creation,
You made me a son to Khan Manas,
And made me slaughter armies and leave widows.
You made me crush stones into roads,
And made me a mighty man of fame
To whom the whole world granted no mercy.
I set fire to river valleys,
And kindled the grass-covered plains,
I poured blood from black mouths,
And crushed all who confronted me.
Yet unable to draw my blade from its sheath,
Tormented and outraged,
Hard-pressed by a loathsome foe,
Külchoro, though his soul was buried in grief,
Could not kill him himself.
With nowhere to flee,
And no grave in which to lie,
O famous land of Talas, your hills are gold and plains are orchards!
O my renowned land of Talas!
Your young are playful and your people golden,
O my beloved Kyrgyz people!
My people, how have I come to see this?” he cried.
“The hero’s strength has left my arms;
Sarybai has slain me.”
His burning soul became an ember,
And Külchoro groaned,
Halting because he could endure no more.
That hero born greater
Than his father, fierce Manas,
That spirit-aided lion,
Had faced many wrestlers.
Against the infidel Sarybai
He had unleashed a mighty conflict.
They stood face-to-face,
Fighting by turns.
When they struck with iron-headed clubs,
Fire flew from their helmets,
And sparks sprang from their maces.
Spears shattered and heroes died,
As they stood face-to-face,
Firing muskets and loosing arrows,
Battering one another to a pulp.
Weary of wielding spears,
They drove their aimless weapons
Into whatever place they struck.
All the mountains became hollows,
And every body was bruised and mangled.
The enraged infidel,
The warrior who devastated nations—
His strength and lionhearted courage
Proclaimed an age like the end of time.
I have seen men and giants,
I have seen nations of every kind,
I have seen champions and lions,
I have seen a man-born hero
Who was the pillar of the whole world.
I wrestled with the mighty,
And contended with devourers of multitudes;
I was wounded and struck by bullets,
Yet never saw fury like this,
And always returned alive and well.
Now my strength is exhausted, my power gone;
Have I withered like white tumbleweed?
At my departure, treacherous world,
Have you truly diminished me?
My heart and head became embers,
I burned, I blazed, I became fire;
My courage fled and drained away.
The enraged Sarybai
Seemed about to seize and hurl aside
The fierce lion born of the magnanimous hero.
Sarybai, son of the ogress,
Flamed like a demon haunting the summer pastures,
As though he would swallow any soul who approached.
If you grappled with him,
He seemed certain to crush your precious life;
When he strained in his madness,
He seemed able to destroy the whole world.
You created him long ago,
Made him a lion greater than Mount Kap,
And in the end, with Sarybai,
You made Sarybai a hero,
But laid the stately princely lion
Level with the black earth!
I burned, I blazed, I became an ember,
I was seared, consumed, and brought to a halt.
Once a cliff, I became level ground;
Unable to prevail against Sarybai,
I became a man bereft of spirit.
Among all mortal sons ever born,
If told to drink water, I drank poison;
If challenged to battle, I spilled blood.
Through many clashes with condemned foes,
I broke many ribs.
Called the warrior son of Manas,
I was mightiest of all creation;
Unable to prevail against Sarybai,
My strength failed and I was disgraced.
You made all twelve parts of my body whole,
And from the time of my earliest forefathers
Made me a spirit-aided lion;
Yet unable to overcome the wrathful foe,
You have cast me into this very disgrace.
You made me a hero before all others,
Yet in the end you laid me
Level with the black earth.
Scorching the face of the land,
Will Sarybai, son of the ogress,
Seize the land where I was born?
Will all our descendants be slaughtered,
And the Kyrgyz remain as plunder?
He is the accursed one himself,
The very eye of wrath,
The moment when true death arrives,
The very calamity itself.
He comes filling every pass
And every mountain saddle;
With every step Sarybai
Comes on ever stronger.
He rumbled and raged,
Growing stronger and more terrible;
Courage departed from the hero,
And this vain created world
Seemed a handful of lies.
My dear ones are bleeding,
My stalwarts are weakening,
My wild colts have grown timid,
My lion warrior stands bewildered.
